title: MSFT Stock Surges Above $556 to Record Highs as Midterms Lift Microsoft and Big Tech - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft shares have rallied above $557 to a new record after recovering from a decline toward $500, as strong cloud growth and improving sentiment following the U.S. midterm elections support buyers, despite growing scrutiny of infrastructure spending and future computing commitments. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have staged a sharp recovery after falling toward $500, with the stock extending its gains today to break above $557 and establish a new record high. The rebound follows renewed concerns about the company’s relationship with Anthropic, rising infrastructure costs and the substantial investment required to expand its computing capacity. Improving sentiment across technology stocks following the U.S. midterm elections has provided another catalyst. Investors are reassessing the potential impact of political pressure on data-centre construction, particularly as electricity costs, grid stability and water consumption become increasingly important issues. Greater regulatory scrutiny could force hyperscalers to reconsider the pace of infrastructure expansion. Although this could create operational challenges, investors may also view more disciplined spending as positive for free cash flow, which has become a major concern across the technology sector. The removal of election uncertainty has also allowed markets to refocus on corporate earnings, economic conditions and the outlook for large technology companies. However, the implications of the election results for tariffs, fiscal negotiations and government policy remain uncertain. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results demonstrated continued strength across its core operations. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue increased to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while earnings comfortably exceeded the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Despite the strong performance, the market reaction highlighted a growing distinction between earnings growth and the returns generated from infrastructure investment. Investors are increasingly questioning whether Microsoft’s spending commitments can translate into sustainable profitability and sufficient cash generation. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. The performance highlights continued demand for cloud computing services and Microsoft’s ability to attract enterprise customers. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. CEO Satya Nadella also highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, expanding cloud capacity requires substantial investment in data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors. The challenge is ensuring that revenue growth keeps pace with capital expenditure rather than allowing infrastructure costs to weaken margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone, revering lower. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments to Microsoft through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. The disclosure relates to an existing arrangement amended during 2026 and highlights the scale of future computing demand. However, large commitments do not eliminate the risks associated with financing and infrastructure expansion. Smaller cloud providers could face greater pressure if borrowing costs remain elevated or customer demand fails to meet expectations. Recent warnings from Elon Musk about the sustainability of some infrastructure businesses have added to concerns about debt-funded data-centre construction. Microsoft has a stronger financial position than many smaller competitors, but it still needs to demonstrate that these commitments will generate attractive returns. Microsoft is also investing in its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver significantly higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and improve infrastructure efficiency. However, development, deployment and scaling require substantial investment before those benefits become fully visible. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the status of those discussions remains unclear. Not every division is experiencing the same momentum. Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%. Regulatory pressure also remains a consideration. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace could add further pressure as businesses reassess subscription costs and available alternatives. The move above $557 marks a significant recovery from the recent decline toward $500. Strong earnings, 30% Microsoft Cloud growth and substantial future computing demand continue to support the company’s fundamentals. However, the central question remains whether Microsoft’s infrastructure commitments and custom-chip investments can deliver sufficient returns. The latest rally suggests buyers are regaining confidence, but elevated spending, financing risks and regulatory scrutiny remain important considerations as the stock enters record territory.

 started its new fiscal year with a quarter that exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. The headline figure was Azure, the company's cloud platform, which grew even faster than in the prior quarter. Management said demand continues to exceed available capacity, a message that suggests the AI build-out has further to run. Azure is now Microsoft's single biggest business line, a remarkable shift for a company once defined by Windows and Office. Growth accelerated on demand for AI training and inference workloads, along with steady migration of traditional enterprise applications to the cloud. The broader Microsoft Cloud division also accelerated. Management described a fast start to the fiscal year and pointed to customers committing to larger, longer contracts. Commercial productivity cloud revenue continued to grow steadily, helped by the rollout of AI assistants across productivity software. The commercial remaining performance obligation, a measure of contracted revenue not yet recognised, surged to a record. This backlog provides unusual visibility and shows that customers are locking in cloud and AI capacity for years ahead rather than paying for short-term needs. Microsoft reorganised its reporting into an Agents and Infra unit, which captures much of the cloud and AI business, and a Devices and Consumer unit. The infrastructure side grew strongly, while devices and consumer revenue slipped, reflecting softer demand for Windows hardware and gaming. The new structure makes the company's priorities clear. Most incremental revenue and profit now comes from cloud infrastructure and AI agents sold to enterprises, while consumer products play a supporting role. To meet demand, Microsoft continues to invest heavily in data centers, chips and networking. Capital expenditures roughly doubled from a year earlier, and management signalled a large spending plan for the full fiscal year. Unlike some peers, Microsoft's operating cash flow still comfortably covers this investment. Reported profit was also boosted by gains linked to its investment in a leading AI model developer, which widened the gap between reported and adjusted growth. Investors generally focus on adjusted figures for a cleaner view of underlying performance. Guidance pointed to continued strong growth in the coming quarter, with Azure expected to grow at a similar or slightly faster pace in constant currency. Management again said capacity constraints remain, meaning revenue growth is partly limited by how quickly new data centers come online. That is an unusual position for a company of Microsoft's scale. It implies demand is not the bottleneck; supply is. As new facilities open, the company expects to convert more of its backlog into revenue. The scale of investment is the main concern. If AI demand slows, or pricing for AI services falls faster than expected, returns on new data centers may disappoint. Power availability, chip supply and regulatory scrutiny of large technology platforms are further factors to monitor. Competition is also intensifying. Rival cloud platforms reported strong growth this season, and custom chips from cloud providers are changing the economics of AI infrastructure. Microsoft's broad enterprise relationships remain a powerful advantage, but no platform has the market to itself. Beyond infrastructure, Microsoft is pushing AI agents into everyday business software. Tools that draft documents, summarise meetings and automate routine tasks are being bundled into enterprise subscriptions, giving the company new ways to raise revenue per user. Adoption across large organisations is still building, but management sees it as a long-term growth layer on top of the cloud. Developer tools and security products also benefit from AI features, strengthening the overall ecosystem and making it harder for customers to switch providers once their workflows are built around Microsoft platforms. The partnership with a leading AI model developer remains a significant strategic asset. It gives Microsoft early access to advanced models for its cloud and software products, while the developer relies on Azure capacity for training and serving its systems, deepening ties between the two organisations. As a heavyweight in the Nasdaq Composite, Microsoft's results help set the tone for the entire technology sector. This quarter offered reassurance that enterprise demand for cloud and AI services remains robust, even as markets debate the overall size of AI spending. The next reports are likely to focus on how quickly capacity expands, whether Azure growth stays near current levels and how AI assistants translate into broader software revenue. For now, the company enters its fiscal year with clear momentum. The arrangement centres on Azure, Microsoft's cloud platform, and on the idea that the cables, gateways and routing layers linking an enterprise's sites, data centres and clouds should be planned at the same time as the cloud and AI projects that depend on them. The update is relevant for readers who follow Bluechip Stocks. The announcement was published on Microsoft's own news site and reads as a commercial alignment rather than a financial transaction. Microsoft is a constituent of the [Dow Jones Industrial Average], the S&P 500, the Nasdaq Composite, the [Nasdaq 100] and the Russell 1000. No price, contract size, launch date or revenue expectation was disclosed. Instead, the companies described joint account planning, a set of Lumen networking capabilities heading toward Azure and Microsoft Marketplace, and a product, Alkira, that is already listed for order through the marketplace today. The companies said they are expanding a collaboration so that their sales teams can pursue enterprise customers together where network modernization, migration to Azure and AI adoption overlap. In practice that means shared account planning and a commitment to find more Lumen capabilities that can be offered through Azure and the Microsoft Marketplace over time. AI systems are only as useful as the data they can reach. Large organisations typically keep information in several public clouds, in private data centres, in branch offices and in partner environments, and the links between those places were often built a project at a time. The announcement describes that patchwork as fragmented and complex, and treats it as a brake on AI deployment. Lumen said it plans to make its cloud networking and application connectivity suite available through Microsoft's cloud and AI ecosystem. The company's pitch rests on network scale and control that customers can switch on as needed, which contrasts with the older model of ordering a fixed circuit and waiting for installation. A concrete item appears in the announcement: Alkira, described as a Lumen Connect solution, is available through Microsoft Marketplace as an ordering option for cloud-native networking. Alkira provides software that orchestrates connections across clouds, sites and data centres, and, combined with Lumen's network, gives enterprises a single portal to connect, secure and manage hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Katy Brown, a corporate vice president for Americas markets and industries at Microsoft, said the company is committed to giving customers choice as they connect existing environments to Azure. She said the work with Lumen helps customers line up network transformation with their cloud and AI priorities. The companies are not new to each other. In the summer of an earlier year they announced a strategic partnership under which Microsoft would use Lumen's network to expand capacity and connectivity between its data centres, while Lumen would use Microsoft's cloud for its own digital transformation. Lumen's Private Connectivity Fabric was named as a key product in that earlier arrangement. Microsoft released its quarterly results a few days earlier, showing revenue growth at a strong pace, operating earnings up sharply and Azure growing by nearly half. Microsoft is among the largest companies listed in the United States, and readers following Bluechip Stocks will recognise it as a standard example of a mega-capitalisation technology business whose product news arrives frequently and often with limited financial detail. Items like this one rarely move reported numbers on their own. For a chief information officer, the practical change would be fewer separate conversations. Today a company planning to move a major application to Azure may speak with its cloud account team about compute and storage, then with a carrier about circuits, and then with a security vendor about traffic inspection. The release does not state when additional Lumen capabilities will reach Azure, nor which ones are prioritised. title: Texas Goes Blue: What Gina Hinojosa's Win Means For AI Data Centers And Stocks Like MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, CRWV - Stocktwits
content: In a major shakeup, Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, toppling one of the nation’s most prominent Republican governors and supporters of President Donald Trump, Greg Abbott. Dem. James Talarico won the state’s Senate seat, defeating Rep. Ken Paxton. The elections are significant as Hinojosa is seen to be critical of the breakneck buildout of AI data centers, a key part of the AI boom that is bringing billions of dollars in sales for chip, infrastructure and software companies. In July, Hinojosa called for a temporary Texas-wide pause on new data centers until lawmakers pass protections. Her proposals include requiring data centers to pay for transmission infrastructure, screening projects for grid impacts, ending tax breaks and giving communities more say. She has repeated the calls during her campaign. Investors and analysts believe a pause or added costs could slow new data center construction and, in turn, constrain AI computing capacity. They fear that a major Democratic win could strengthen the growing nationwide push for data center restrictions. Texas is home to data centers operated by Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, as well as AI campuses developed by Crusoe for customers including OpenAI, Oracle, Microsoft and Google. Several companies are expanding or building new Texas campuses. Democrats have won control of the U.S. Senate and are on the brink of taking the House in a widespread repudiation of Trump, according to the latest reporting by the Associated Press. Official certification of results comes weeks later. Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in, with cloud stocks dropping sharply overnight. Hyperscalers Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT), and Alphabet (GOOGL) fell 0.4% to 1% ahead of Wednesday, while Oracle (ORCL) fell sharply by 2.3%. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave (CRWV) and Iren Ltd. (IREN) dropped 3.3% and 4.3%, respectively, while Applied Digital (APLD) slid 3%. Among chipmakers, Intel (INTC) slid 0.7% while Nvidia (NVDA) was flat. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a cheeky post on X. Some commentators, however, said concerns about slowing data center buildout were overblown or already priced in by investors. “If companies ask for no subsidies, promise a ton of union jobs, and guarantee that water and electricity costs won't rise/plus add supply, data centers can be built under her governorship,” said "Key Context" newsletter author Tae Kim in an X post, referring to a proposed concessions on Hinojosa’s website. “Data centers will come under scrutiny but that fear has been adequately priced in at this point. Many Republicans campaigned on tighter permitting too,” Michael Sikand, a trader and founder of financial media company Our Future, said in an X post. According to trading firm Liquid, Iren and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) have substantial Texas exposure through projects such as Sweetwater and Helios, making the treatment of future expansion especially important. Nebius and Applied Digital have less direct exposure, with their disclosed core AI campuses outside Texas. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ for GOOGL and AMZN, ‘bullish’ for MSFT, and ‘bearish’ for META. The sentiment was ‘bearish’ for CRWV, APLD and IREN. “$CRWV results of the mid term will have little effect on tech stock long terms. Tech companies have survived administrations under both parties,” a trader said. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. SpaceX (SPCX), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) and Rocket Lab (RKLB) shares fell overnight as fears of political backlash against Elon Musk following Democratic midterm gains spilled into the broader space sector, raising fresh questions about a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger. SPCX, RKLB, ASTS, Planet Labs (PL), Redwire (RDW) and Intuitive Machines (LUNR) all fell between 2% and 6% overnight heading into Wednesday. Democrats won the Senate and are projected to take the House, raising the prospect of tougher scrutiny of Musk’s government dealings. The selling also swept the wider market: Nasdaq futures fell 0.4% and S&P 500 futures slid 0.3%, and Dow futures slipped 0.1% heading into Wednesday trade. Satellite communications and spectrum consultant Tim Farrar raised the prospect of Musk shifting the spotlight from politics to business. “Will Musk/SpaceX announce some business deal tomorrow to change the focus away from politics?” he asked on X. His doubts come after a recent note in which he speculated that SpaceX could pursue EchoStar’s remaining business through a share-based deal involving wireless assets and spectrum. Meanwhile, Alexandra Merz, CEO of L&F Investor Services, questioned Musk’s political spending: “First time I see Elon not making good on the money he invests.” Musk contributed $446 million during the 2026 midterm election cycle, mostly to Republican-aligned groups. Musk’s ties to Trump and his former role leading DOGE have raised the stakes, with Democrats threatening investigations into his government work and federal contracts. Lawmakers have also sought a probe into reported SpaceX communications restrictions in Ukraine. Trump recently signaled willingness to consider pre-emptive pardons for Musk and other allies, saying: “I would if I needed to, sure. I wouldn’t even think about it. I did it for J6.” Merz said Democratic gains could bring more hearings, subpoenas and scrutiny of government contracts, complicating a Tesla-SpaceX merger without automatically blocking it. “Congress cannot simply veto a private merger,” she said. “It does not, by itself, put the merger off the table.” She identified shareholder approval, special-committee processes and regulatory reviews as the key hurdles. Both companies have formed committees to assess a merger. Merz pointed to committee progress, potential disclosures ahead of Tesla’s Dec.3 annual meeting and formal deal terms as the next developments to watch. Veteran investor George Noble urged adding to his bearish bets on Musk’s companies. “Elon Musk is the biggest loser in the elections tonight. TIME to add to our profitable short positions in $SPCX and $TSLA,” he said on X. “The speed of the coming collapse will be something to behold.” Last month, Noble called Tesla and SpaceX short calls at $485 and $145, respectively, pointing to cash burn, heavy spending and high valuations. He acknowledged then that Tesla had fallen since his call, while SpaceX had risen. “The election doesn’t solve the AI funding problem.” Cardone Capital founder and CEO Grant Cardone also flagged political risks: “If talarico wins Texas it won’t be good for SpaceX or the AI bet.” Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, ending Democrats’ statewide losing streak in Texas dating to 1994. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley offered a bullish counterpoint, as per a note shared by Tesla investor and influencer Sawyer Merritt. “On fiscal year 2028, $SPCX trades cheaper than the S&P500. Interesting,” the firm said. Using a $140 reference share price and projected 2028 adjusted earnings of $109 billion, the research firm put SpaceX at 17.6 times estimated earnings, just below the S&P 500’s estimated 17.7 times multiple. He nearly doubled his 2027 revenue forecast to $175 billion and raised his 2028 revenue and operating-income estimates to $289 billion and $119 billion, respectively. “At the time of our initiation, we had expected SPCX to be FCF negative until 2035. Today, we forecast the company to achieve positive FCF by 2031 - a 4 year pull-forward FCF break-even,” Morgan Stanley said. Projected borrowing fell to $390 billion through 2031 from $670 billion through 2035, though the forecasts cover different periods. On Stocktwits, sentiment for SPCX, ASTS and RKLB was ‘bearish,’ with ‘low’ message activity across all three stocks. One user said, “That’s why EM [Elon Musk] should have stayed out of politics, now you tie your share price to the political landscape.” Another user said that Musk’s critics in a Democratic-led Congress could favor funding and contracts for companies outside his business empire. AST buys SpaceX launch services while competing in satellite-based mobile connectivity. Rocket Lab competes with SpaceX for launches and supplies spacecraft and components to government customers, giving the companies different exposure to Musk’s political risks. A separate user urged investors to hold their positions, citing historically strong market performance in the third year of a presidential term. U.S. President Donald Trump claimed Republicans would have won a landslide had he been on the ballot as Democrats captured the Senate and projected to win the House, while market strategists warned of gridlock and growing risks for AI investors. Election-night nerves turned trading screens red: the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) fell 0.8%, the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) lost 1.2% and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) slipped 0.5% overnight heading into Wednesday. The selloff extended to index futures, with Dow futures down 0.3%, S&P 500 futures off 0.6%, and Nasdaq-100 futures about 0.8% lower. Trump Media & Technology Group (DJT) also fell overnight, tumbling over 6% to $6.30. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump said on Truth Social as Republican losses mounted Tuesday. The claim followed his appeal just days earlier for supporters to treat the midterms as a vote on his presidency. At a weekend rally in Dubuque, Iowa, he told voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” putting his leadership at the heart of the campaign. Democrats secured Senate control after flipping Republican-held seats in six states. Roy Cooper won in North Carolina, James Talarico in Texas, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Josh Turek in Iowa. The party was also projected to win a House majority, putting Democrats in position to challenge Trump’s agenda across both chambers. Counting continues, with final seat totals still unsettled. Before posting his landslide claim, Trump struck a more conciliatory tone in a late-Tuesday interview. “I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he said, expressing willingness to cooperate with Democrats and adding: “We’ll probably work something out.” World Trade Securities CEO Nicholas Mugalli warned about the election’s potential market fallout. “Tonight is an absolute bloodbath for all investors especially AI investors,” he said on X. Mugalli pointed to Texas’ importance as a hub for AI data centers, warning that Democratic gains could bring tougher regulation. He also criticized Trump’s handling of inflation and living costs. Carson Group Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick raised broader concerns about the prospect of a Republican president facing a Democratic Congress. “The worst possible combination is a Republican President and a Democratic Congress. Futures seem to agree so far,” he said on X. GLJ Research analyst Gordon Johnson called the Democratic Senate takeover a surprise, saying the Washington consultants he follows had either viewed control as a toss-up or expected Republicans to hold the chamber. “NONE of them predicted the Democrats would take the Senate,” he said on X. “No matter what ANYONE tells you, this is 100% a surprise.” Other forecasters had seen a stronger Democratic outlook. Before the vote, polling analyst Nate Silver’s model gave the party an 80% chance of winning the Senate, while his election-day analysis called Democrats clear favorites for the House. Silver linked Republicans’ troubles to Trump’s unpopularity, the Iran war, fuel prices and public anxiety about AI data centers. “All of these problems are Trump’s fault. He almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms,” Silver said before the results. Historian Allan Lichtman also anticipated big Democratic gains. “I am expecting a net gain of 40 U.S. House and 6 U.S. Senate seats. Let’s see how close we get,” he said on X. Infowars founder Alex Jones portrayed Republican losses as a major blow to Trump’s political coalition. In an X post, he quoted Richard Baris, a pollster and managing director of Big Data Poll: “This Is A Beating That Will Keep Republicans Out Of The Senate For 10 Years!” Jones added: “THE TRUMP COALITION HAS BEEN OBLITERATED!” Meanwhile, economist Peter Schiff saw a different consequence: Democratic victories could give Trump someone to blame if the economy deteriorates. “Since the Democrats swept the midterms, Trump has the scapegoat he needs for the coming economic collapse,” Schiff wrote on X, calling the outcome a sweep. Former Goldman Sachs strategist Robin Brooks turned to the potential fallout beyond Washington, questioning whether Democratic gains could increase the likelihood of renewed fighting with Iran. “I think it raises the odds of war,” he said. Brooks also linked the risk to the outlook for oil and precious metals. James Thorne, chief market strategist at Wellington-Altus, said that a divided government could preserve much of Trump’s economic agenda, even as it makes new legislation harder to pass. “If Democrats control the House and Senate with a Republican president, the Hamiltonian economic agenda stays largely intact,” he said. “Gridlock freezes the existing framework.” Thorne said existing tax provisions, production incentives and tariffs would be difficult to unwind. He viewed the election as a demand to tackle affordability and end the Iran conflict. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Joby Aviation (JOBY) stock is drawing attention ahead of its third-quarter (Q3) earnings as ARK Invest analyst Tasha Keeney sees autonomous electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft eventually offering fares competitive with traditional taxis. Joby Aviation stock traded over 2% lower overnight, heading into Wednesday. The stock has been declining for the past five months. In an X post, ARK Invest analyst Daniel Maguire recalled how St. Petersburg hosted the first commercial airline journey in 1914. Pilot Tony Jannus carried former St. Petersburg Mayor Abram Fail to Tampa Bay in about 23 minutes. Fail paid $400 for the trip, equivalent to more than $10,000 in 2026 dollars. The experimental airline service operated for three months, giving the industry important lessons about running commercial flights. More than a century later, the same Florida waterfront hosted a demonstration of an electric aircraft developed by Joby Aviation. Keeney said a drive that normally requires about 45 minutes took the aircraft less than half that time. The demonstration offered an early look at how electric aircraft could change short-distance transportation, particularly in cities where road travel frequently slows down. “In the future, we expect that eVTOLs that are autonomously operated could price competitively with today's human-driven taxi cabs.” She also pointed to the possibility of widespread ground-based robotaxis, which could reduce transportation costs per mile but potentially increase the number of vehicles on roads. If cheaper autonomous rides lead to heavier traffic, journeys that already take 45 minutes could become even longer. Keeney added that electric aircraft could benefit from that situation by offering passengers a way to avoid busy roads while reaching their destinations in considerably less time. Last week, ARK Invest made a string of JOBY share purchases through two of its exchange-traded funds (ETFs), ARK Autonomous Technology & Robotics ETF (ARKQ) and ARK Space Exploration & Innovation ETF (ARKX), signaling conviction in the company’s commercial flight trials. Joby has gained momentum following its active involvement in the FAA’s Electric Powered-lift Integration Program (eIPP).  The company’s second-quarter revenue jumped 56% to $39 million. title: MSFT Stock Rebounds Above $520 as Microsoft's Anthropic Commitment Reaches $44.9 Billion - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft shares have recovered sharply after falling toward $500, reclaiming losses with a 3% rebound as investors assess a reported $44.9 billion Anthropic computing commitment against rising infrastructure costs, custom-chip investment and growing concerns about the returns from data-centre expansion. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have experienced significant volatility after initially climbing above $550 in mid-October following stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings. However, the rally quickly reversed, with the stock falling toward $500 on Monday as investors reassessed infrastructure spending and the financial returns from expanding computing capacity. The decline followed renewed pressure across technology stocks after Apple’s and Palantir’s earnings, although Microsoft has recovered sharply on Tuesday, gaining approximately 3% and reclaiming the $520 level. The rebound comes as investors digest new disclosures concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic. An amended filing identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments to Microsoft through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. The disclosure highlights the scale of future computing demand, although it relates to an existing arrangement amended during 2026. The recovery also comes ahead of the US midterm elections, which could influence broader market sentiment and expectations surrounding technology regulation, government spending and economic policy. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, representing a 32% increase year over year on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue increased to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, meeting analyst expectations, while earnings comfortably exceeded the consensus forecast of $4.27 per share. Despite the strong results, the market reaction demonstrated that investors are becoming more demanding. Earnings growth alone may no longer be sufficient to justify Microsoft’s premium valuation if infrastructure expenses continue increasing faster than expected returns. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. CEO Satya Nadella also highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, investors want evidence that strong cloud demand can translate into sustainable profitability. Expanding data-centre capacity requires substantial capital, and the financial benefits depend on how quickly Microsoft can monetise that investment. The reported $44.9 billion commitment from Anthropic provides an important indication of the potential demand for Microsoft’s computing infrastructure. However, the broader industry faces questions about financing and the sustainability of spending. Elon Musk recently warned that smaller cloud infrastructure providers could struggle to survive as competition increases and financing becomes more difficult. His comments reflect concerns that companies relying heavily on debt to finance data-centre construction could face pressure if customer demand or revenue growth fails to meet expectations. For Microsoft, the challenge is balancing substantial future commitments with the need to maintain attractive margins and generate sufficient cash flow. Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver significantly higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually reduce Microsoft’s infrastructure costs, although development and deployment require substantial investment before the benefits become visible. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the status of those discussions remains unclear. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again yesterday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in yellow in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone, revering lower. Not all divisions are delivering the same growth. Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, declining 3% year over year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%. Regulatory pressure is another concern. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace could also challenge Microsoft’s business software operations as companies reassess subscription costs and available alternatives. Microsoft’s latest rebound above $520 suggests buyers are returning after the stock approached $500. Strong cloud growth and the Anthropic commitment provide evidence of continued demand for computing infrastructure. However, the larger challenge remains profitability. Investors are increasingly questioning whether enormous data-centre investments can generate sufficient returns to justify current valuations. A sustained recovery will depend on Microsoft’s ability to convert cloud demand into stronger cash generation while controlling infrastructure costs. Without clearer evidence of improving investment returns, the stock could remain vulnerable to further volatility despite its strong underlying earnings.

title: PLTR Stock Gets Fresh Price Target Hikes, But Jefferies Favors MSFT, ORCL, SNOW Shares - Stocktwits
content: Palantir Technologies (PLTR) shares fell in morning trading on Tuesday, putting the stock on track to hit its lowest level since September, even as analysts raised their price targets following the company’s third-quarter results. Citi, Morgan Stanley, Piper Sandler and RBC Capital all lifted their targets, but Jefferies kept its target steady at $80 with an ‘Underperform’ rating, according to TheFly. The firm said that while Palantir delivered a "strong" quarter, the debate has shifted from whether customers want Palantir’s software to whether the company can sustain accelerating growth against tougher comparisons. Jefferies said it sees “more compelling” risk and reward elsewhere in Microsoft (MSFT), Oracle (ORCL), and Snowflake (SNOW). According to the firm, they offer strong long-term growth at more attractive valuations. PLTR stock dropped around 5% in morning trade and was among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Palantir reported revenue growth accelerating for the 13th consecutive quarter. Revenue grew 96% year over year in the third quarter (Q3) to $2.31 billion, beating market expectations of $2.17 billion, according to Koyfin. The company also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $8.53 billion from about $8.15 billion, its third increase this year. It expects fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue of about $2.65 billion. Citi, which raised its target to $265 from $250 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating, called the results “another top-line blowout,” driven by U.S. commercial and government sales. Morgan Stanley analyst Sanjit Singh called revenue growth for a 13th consecutive quarter “impressive.” The main concern for Wall Street was bookings, which indicate future business. Total contract value (TCV), which measures the value of deals signed during the quarter, rose 6% year over year to $2.92 billion, down sharply from 49% growth in the second quarter. U.S. commercial TCV increased 11%. According to Morgan Stanley, PLTR stock’s reaction reflected elevated expectations for U.S. commercial sales and slower bookings growth linked to shorter contracts. Meanwhile, RBC Capital highlighted remaining deal value grew just 2% from the second quarter, while remaining performance obligations (RPO) were flat sequentially. The firm also noted management’s acknowledgment that contracts tied to Sovereign AI, Palantir’s work with national governments, were shorter than usual. Piper Sandler said investors will look for evidence in coming quarters that the 11% growth in U.S. commercial bookings “is a fluke of duration and not something structural.” The firm believes the slowdown is related to contract length and said demand for Palantir’s software still “very much outstrip[s] supply.” Citi also described the quarter as strong “despite a duration headwind to bookings.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around PLTR stock flipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ over the past day, while chatter increased to ‘extremely high’ from ‘normal’ levels. Platform data showed an over 1,100% increase in message volume over the past 24 hours. Some retail traders pushed back against concerns over Palantir's valuation and growth outlook, with some pointing to what they saw as a shift in the criticism of Palantir's business mix. If the PLTR stock's decline holds through the regular session, the shares would give up their year-to-date gains. Veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warned Monday that a Democratic sweep in Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections could deliver a “cold shower for stocks,” arguing that investors have yet to fully price in that possibility. Yardeni said political gridlock could become damaging paralysis, complicating government spending and debt-ceiling negotiations. Prolonged fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher and weigh on equity valuations, he added. He also argued that a Democratic-controlled Congress might do little to constrain President Donald Trump's use of executive authority, citing tariffs and military action against Iran. However, Yardeni said he would view a significant market selloff as a buying opportunity, given the strength of the U.S. economy and corporate earnings. UBS Global Wealth Management assigned a 50% probability to a Democratic sweep, a 40% chance of Democrats winning the House while Republicans retain the Senate, and a 10% probability of Republicans retaining both chambers. In its Monday report, UBS said changes in congressional control could complicate fiscal negotiations, with debt-ceiling discussions in 2027 potentially creating volatility. However, the bank said that narrow congressional majorities and presidential veto power should limit sweeping legislation, while Trump would retain considerable authority over tariffs, foreign policy, and regulation. UBS also expects Treasury yields to settle slightly lower over the next 12 months as easing inflation should outweigh persistent fiscal concerns. The bank said it “would not treat the midterms as a binary directional event” for markets, emphasizing that earnings, economic growth, AI investment and interest rates remain more important drivers. The election also comes amid a pullback in AI stocks. However, UBS does not expect a change in congressional control to derail data-center expansion, as many relevant decisions are made at state and local levels. According to a Reuters report, Citigroup U.S. equity strategist Scott Chronert said stocks would likely react positively if Republicans retained control of the Senate, but negatively if Democrats secured a larger-than-expected Senate majority. “Investors are going into the midterms very cautious,” Indosuez Wealth Management Chief Investment Officer Alexandre Drabowicz told Bloomberg, adding that market fundamentals remain strong and the S&P 500 has historically resumed climbing after elections. title: Bill Ackman on MSFT, AMZN and META: Why Big Tech's Trillion-Dollar AI Spend Is 'Offensive Rather Than Defensive' - TradingView
content: Bill Ackman‘s Pershing Square Inc. PS has said that the artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditures by Microsoft Corp. MSFT, Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, and Meta Platforms Inc. META are designed to accelerate growth. In a recent shareholder letter, the executives described the projected trillion-dollar outlay by major technology companies as “offensive rather than defensive.” Addressing investor concerns regarding the returns on elevated spending by the hyperscalers, Chief Executive Officer William Ackman and Chief Investment Officer Ryan Israel wrote, “We believe that the hyperscalers’ capital spending is offensive rather than defensive.” The executives stated that “Rather than merely protecting existing franchises, we believe the hyperscalers are investing to accelerate growth and are deploying capital behind a transformative technology that plays directly to their competitive advantages.” The letter detailed how these investments are impacting specific portfolio companies. Regarding AMZN, the executives wrote that “Amazon is extremely well positioned across the AI stack.” They noted that “AI has helped AWS accelerate its revenue growth to 39% in the third quarter.” For META, the letter stated that “Meta’s core digital advertising business has effectively used AI for better ad targeting, generative ad copy, and more effective content recommendation.” Ackman and Israel also noted, “By frontloading its compute investment, Meta has given itself the optionality to scale Muse to a billion or more users.” Regarding MSFT, the executives stated, “Microsoft occupies an enviable position among the hyperscalers in having two large channels by which to monetize its compute.” They noted that “the narrative on the stock has shifted from the company being an AI laggard to an AI leader.” Beyond the hyperscalers, Ackman and Israel highlighted what they view as mispriced opportunities in other portfolio companies. Regarding Uber Technologies Inc. UBER, the executives noted the stock now trades at “its lowest valuation ever.” They stated that investor concerns regarding autonomous vehicles are “increasingly disconnected from its strong business performance.” Ackman and Israel wrote that “the risk due to AVs is minimal,” and projected that Uber’s earnings per share will “compound at 25% or more for the foreseeable future.” Addressing Netflix Inc. NFLX, the letter noted that recent stock declines were driven by investor concerns over plateauing engagement. However, the executives argued that measuring engagement solely by watch time “overshadows the quality of that engagement, which is what ultimately drives the value proposition for Netflix subscribers.” Ackman and Israel concluded that the market “vastly undervalues the company’s growth profile and business quality.” The letter acknowledged concerns over how these companies will fund their infrastructure buildout. Ackman and Israel noted that the hyperscalers are “collectively expected to spend a little over $1 trillion on capital expenditures in 2027 based on consensus estimates.” However, the executives concluded that “The hyperscalers are in a vastly stronger financial position,” adding that they “can finance the substantial majority of their capital expenditures from the prodigious cash flows of their core businesses.” This content was partially produced with the help of AI tools and was reviewed and published by Benzinga editors. The push toward custom silicon marks a notable shift for a company long known for software and cloud services rather than chip design. Designing accelerators tuned to its own data-center workloads allows tighter integration between hardware and the services running across the cloud, and it reflects a broader move among large operators toward purpose-built compute. The step also reflects the sheer scale of demand the company is managing. Running expansive model training and inference across a global cloud footprint places enormous weight on compute efficiency, and building silicon tailored to those workloads offers a path to greater control over performance and energy use. At the center of the narrative sits the company cloud engine, which has grown into among the largest platforms serving enterprise computing. The cloud arm has carried much of the demand tied to the artificial intelligence buildout, hosting the training and inference workloads that have reshaped data-center spending across the market. That cloud footprint gives the custom-silicon move its weight. Every efficiency advance in the hardware beneath the platform compounds across an immense base of servers, and the ability to tune accelerators to the exact shape of cloud workloads offers a meaningful lever. The competitive landscape across cloud and compute has grown dense. Rival hyperscale operators have each pursued their own blend of merchant accelerators and custom designs, and the established chip designers continue to push successive generations of hardware. The company move into homegrown silicon places it alongside peers that have already fielded in-house accelerators. Rather than displacing the merchant chip suppliers outright, the custom-silicon push tends to run in parallel, giving operators a mix of options tuned to different workloads. The step into custom accelerators extends a pattern already visible in earlier in-house chip efforts spanning general-purpose cloud processors and security silicon. Managing the enormous capital commitment tied to data-center expansion has become a defining operational theme. Building facilities, securing power and provisioning compute at the scale required for modern artificial intelligence places heavy demands on planning and execution. title: Alphabet’s $400 Billion Sell-Off Could Be the Best AI Buying Window Left in 2026 - MarketBeat

Investors just sold off a company for spending money on the one business that doubled. Alphabet Inc. NASDAQ: GOOGL fell 12% after its third-quarter report, erasing more than $400 billion in market value. Google Cloud revenue grew 103% in that same quarter. That’s the tension worth sitting with, because the distance between what the market reacted to and what the numbers said is where the opportunity is. The two misses that triggered the selling came from Google Search advertising and YouTube ad revenue. Search ad revenue still grew 12% to $63.3 billion. That is not a franchise being erased by chatbots. That is a franchise compounding slightly slower than the sell-side modeled. Joel Litman and Rob Spivey of Altimetry Research argue the cloud line invalidates the bubble narrative the sell-off was built on. Demand for AI compute is not softening. Customers are spending more with Google, not less. Alphabet booked an $8.2 billion loss in other income and expenses, driven largely by an unrealized mark-to-market loss on its stake in SpaceX NASDAQ: SPCX. No cash left the building. Litman points out that these are precisely the rules Warren Buffett has criticized for manufacturing volatility without conveying information. Research and development compounds the distortion. In the United States, R&D hits the income statement as a period expense rather than a capitalized asset, so the companies investing hardest look the least profitable. Then there is free cash flow, the number that spooked the market most. Alphabet’s turned negative because capital expenditures (CapEx) climbed toward a guided $195 billion to $205 billion for the year, not because operating cash flow deteriorated. Litman and Spivey read that as a company with high incremental returns pressing its advantage. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella has said repeatedly that more Azure capacity would mean more Azure revenue, and each capacity expansion that panicked investors has converted into a cloud revenue beat. The recent voluntary exit offer extended to roughly 60,000 employees reads as distress to much of the financial press. Spivey reads it as leverage. Headcount is an unusually large share of Microsoft’s cost base, and more revenue per employee translates directly into a return on investment lift the market has not priced. Generac Holdings Inc. NYSE: GNRC is the name nobody files under AI. Spivey argues it belongs there. The residential standby business remains dominant, while the commercial segment, historically the lower-margin half, is finally getting pricing power as Caterpillar Inc. NYSE: CAT runs years deep in backlog. Generac added capacity ahead of that squeeze and has built a data center backlog measured in billions. Spivey’s view is that reported metrics understate the economics badly, showing low single-digit returns where Altimetry’s adjusted figures show mid-teens and rising. The stock’s slide since its summer peak, he says, is narrative, not fundamentals. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. NASDAQ: AMD benefits from a simple realization spreading through data centers: not every workload needs NVIDIA Corporation’s NASDAQ: NVDA top-end silicon. Inference is pushing work back toward CPUs, and AMD is the only major designer sitting on both sides of that split with integration between them. CoreWeave, Inc. NASDAQ: CRWV pays top dollar for chips, owns no frontier model, and cannot tell customers they have nowhere else to go. Litman’s calculation is blunt: economic profit is negative today and forecast to stay negative. Cipher Digital Inc. NASDAQ: CIFR, the former Cipher Mining, inherits the same problem with a rebrand attached. Renting bare compute is the business Equinix, Inc. NASDAQ: EQIX and Digital Realty Trust, Inc. NYSE: DLR have run for decades at 3% to 4% returns on assets. The exception is scale paired with power already in the ground, which is why Spivey points to SpaceX and its xAI operation as the only neocloud he considers genuinely differentiated. Owning something the buildout can’t route around is the whole game. Cloud revenue and power capacity tell you who qualifies, and five of those names are already cutting checks to shareholders while the spending runs. title: Bill Ackman Says MSFT, AMZN and NFLX Fit His ‘Enormously Valuable’ 20-Year Investing Test - TradingView

content: Technology stocks saw a busy week as Intel Corp. (INTC) shares plunged on a weak outlook, while Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) strong AI and cloud demand raised investor optimism. Meanwhile, Meta Platforms (META), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), DoorDash Inc. (DASH) and Verizon Communications (VZ) announced major developments. Intel stock crashed 24% after the chipmaker issued a disappointing fourth-quarter (Q4) outlook. Although Q3 revenue climbed 21% year-on-year to $16.5 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.52 per share exceeded expectations, the company warned that supply shortages and declining PC demand would weigh on upcoming results. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company needs to increase production to meet strong demand for its Xeon processors. Data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion, while its Foundry division recorded a 58% increase to $6.7 billion. However, memory shortages and an unexpected shutdown at an Israeli facility disrupted operations. Intel expects PC demand to remain under pressure through at least the first half of 2027. For Q4, it sees revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.25 per share. RBC Capital and Goldman Sachs also reduced their price targets on Intel following the weak outlook. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Microsoft delivered a stronger fiscal Q1 2027 performance, with revenue up 19% to $92.3 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said strong demand for the company’s AI and cloud services drove growth. Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 30% to $63.9 billion, while Azure revenue grew 48%, beating analyst estimates. However, Microsoft increased quarterly spending by 30% to $45.2 billion to build its AI infrastructure. Revenue from its consumer and devices business fell 3%. The company expects Q2 revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion. Baird analyst William Power raised Microsoft's price target to $600 from $500 while maintaining an ‘Outperform’ rating after the results and remains positive about faster growth in Azure and Microsoft 365. The new price target implies a 15% upside from the stock’s last close. Microsoft stock dipped 0.5% over the week, while retail sentiment around the stock slipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’. Meta Platforms moved closer to its consumer robotics ambitions after developing a humanoid prototype called Max with Chinese robotics manufacturer Fourier. According to The Information’s report, the approximately 106-pound machine was developed in three months, and the companies have already started working on another version. The project is part of Meta’s plan to use AI in everyday household tasks. The company sees humanoid robots as a way to bring its Muse AI assistant into the physical world. However, U.S. restrictions and possible new limits on Chinese robotics imports could make development more difficult. Separately, Meta announced a $97.5 billion equity offering plan, including preferred and common stock sales, to support its AI infrastructure expansion and consumer AI products. Nvidia also strengthened its relationship with Meta through a $3 billion investment in the offering and an expanded AI partnership. The two companies plan to improve the training and performance of Meta's Muse platform through Nvidia's computing technology. Meta stock dropped 4% over the week with sentiment remaining ‘bearish’. DoorDash stock edged down 0.2% during the week after announcing an agreement to purchase grocery delivery platform Instacart (CART) for about $17 billion. The deal values Instacart at $65 per share, representing a 26% premium to its Oct. 22 closing price. At least 75% of the payment will consist of cash, while stock consideration will account for no more than 25%. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said the combination could help neighborhood retailers compete with larger online businesses. The companies plan to combine DoorDash's delivery network with Instacart's grocery technology, retailer relationships and fulfillment capabilities. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Adjusted earnings came in at $1.31 per share, beating the $1.27 analyst estimate, although revenue of $34.31 billion missed expectations. The telecom operator added 406,000 postpaid phone customers during the quarter, more than eightfold higher than the previous year. It also generated $7.8 billion in free cash flow, up 12.1% year over year. CEO Dan Schulman addressed the potential competitive threat from SpaceX (SPCX) and its Starlink ambitions. Schulman argued that building a nationwide mobile network would require investment, thousands of cell sites and several years of work. He estimated that such an undertaking could cost between $300 billion and $500 billion over seven to eight years. Retail sentiment around the stock slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘neutral’. A planned venue for trading tokenized U.S. stocks from New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and crypto exchange OKX has hit a wall, as Nvidia (NVDA) and Nike (NKE) joined a growing list of companies objecting to their shares being offered on it. The number of companies objecting to OKXICE tokenizing their shares has grown to 50, journalist Eleanor Terrett said on X on Sunday. She said Nike, Costco (COST), Micron (MU), Reddit (RDDT) and Nvidia were among the new additions. The venture had initially proposed tokenizing shares from 62 companies, Terrett said. The venue's notice listed objectors including Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Goldman Sachs (GS), JPMorgan (JPM), Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ), Intel (INTC) and Walmart (WMT). AI-linked companies like CoreWeave (CRWV), Oracle (ORCL) and Arm Holdings (ARM) were also on it, along with CrowdStrike (CRWD), Corning (GLW), IREN (IREN) and Bloom Energy (BE). The objections piled up quickly. The venue's October 19 notice showed 16 objectors. OKXICE is a 50-50 joint venture between ICE and OKX, and plans to run under a temporary exemption the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued in September, which lets it trade tokenized U.S. stocks without registering as an exchange, according to its public notice. Trading would run 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with each stock paired against a stablecoin, including such as USDC and Tether’s USDT Trades would go through automated liquidity pools on OKX's X Layer blockchain, built on Uniswap (UNI) v4. Billionaire investor Mark Cuban said public companies that audited their health plans found they were being overcharged by insurers such as UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS) and Cigna (CI), but refused to tell shareholders about the findings. On a16z’s podcast on Thursday, Cost Plus Drugs co-founder Cuban said he had asked companies to run their insurance and pharmacy benefit contracts through artificial intelligence before signing them, asking where they were being overcharged and what to do about it. Cuban said a couple of the public companies that took his advice were stunned by the results. “There’s a couple public companies that I told to do this and came back to me and were like, ‘Oh my God, we had no idea how badly we were ripped off.’ I'm begging them to mention it on their quarterly earnings conference calls, and they won't do it because they still have to do business with those [insurers]," he said. Cuban did not name any companies. He supports the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which would require insurers to divest pharmacy benefit managers and provider assets. The problem starts with contracts so long that no one can catch every clause, Cuban said. He cited the city of Dallas, which has a PBM contract that tops 1,300 pages. "There's no group of humans with enough coffee on the planet to be able to catch everything they try to squeeze by," he said. He said that an insurer wins when a company signs terms it doesn't fully understand. No AI can protect it after that. Cuban said that he uses several AI agents to get contracts from school districts, cities and unions by asking for public records. He said the contracts show how these organizations are being overcharged. Cuban said that UnitedHealth has more than 3,000 subsidiaries and that these subsidiaries transfer about $150 billion a year with each other. CVS and Cigna are close behind. He said insurance companies raise premiums and deductibles and send patients to businesses they own. About 60% of people who have health insurance through their jobs get it through self-insured employers, Cuban said. He said that employers often can't figure out what they pay for and what hospitals actually get because the insurers own the administrators that process their claims. He also said insurers' earnings calls never mention lower costs for employers or patients. "They always say this is going to improve our earnings," Cuban said. UNH stock closed 0.9% lower on Friday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around UNH remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, amid ‘low’ chatter levels over the past day. UnitedHealth had its best year since 2021 in October, outpacing healthcare ETFs. Cuban said employers don't need to wait for new laws to cut costs. He said that companies should hire an executive whose only job is to handle healthcare contracts. Cuban said that the system that helps big insurers and PBMs would fall apart if employers covering about 160 million Americans ran their contracts through AI before signing. "The cost of healthcare in this country would drop like a rock," he said. Cybersecurity stocks have emerged as some of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence boom in 2026, with investors betting that the same technology transforming businesses is also creating a new wave of security threats. Okta Inc. (OKTA), CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. (CRWD) and Palo Alto Networks Inc. (PLTR) are up 141%, 114% and 99%, respectively, through Oct. 30. The First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) is also up nearly 40%, far ahead of the Nasdaq 100’s roughly 11% gain. CrowdStrike shares closed more than 4% lower in Friday’s regular trading session, Palo Alto Networks shares fell nearly 4%, while Okta shares fell over 6%. According to IO Fund, the first major driver behind the rally is the growing use of AI in cyberattacks and the expanding attack surface companies now have to defend. CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, cited by IO Fund, found that AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89% in 2025. IBM’s research shows that one in four security breaches is now AI-enabled, with those incidents costing roughly $6 million on average, versus a $4.99 million global average. The threat is also pushing companies to increase spending. IO Fund cited IBM data showing that 85% of organizations plan to raise security spending after learning about the cyber capabilities of frontier AI models, up from 64% in 2025. The shift is becoming particularly important as companies deploy increasingly autonomous AI agents that can write code, access systems and perform tasks with limited human intervention. The firm also pointed to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s warning about the difficulty of securing increasingly capable AI systems: “I no longer think we’re gonna be able to just patch all the bugs,” Altman said during a speech at Stanford Graduate School of Business last month. IO Fund said Gartner expects spending on platforms designed to secure AI systems to climb from about $3 billion in 2026 to $7.7 billion in 2028, suggesting the emerging threat could translate into a substantial new security spending cycle. The other major trend identified by IO Fund is happening inside corporate security departments, which is, customers are increasingly consolidating their spending across broader cybersecurity platforms rather than buying a growing number of point solutions. CrowdStrike’s results offer one indication of the trend, the firm said, adding that CrowdStrike’s annual recurring revenue from its Falcon Flex offering topped $2.2 billion, up 101% year over year, while 51% of its subscription customers now use six or more modules. The firm added that Palo Alto Networks is seeing a similar shift. IO Fund noted that the company added roughly 220 platformization deals in its fiscal fourth quarter (Q4), more than double the pace from two years earlier. Net revenue retention among platformized customers exceeded 120%, while Prisma AIRS, its AI security platform, surpassed $100 million in annual recurring revenue. IO Fund added that AI may not simply create demand for a new category of security products, but it could also accelerate spending with vendors that can secure multiple parts of an enterprise’s infrastructure. IO Fund estimates CrowdStrike’s revenue could grow at a 23% compound annual rate through fiscal 2029, more than twice Gartner’s projected 11% annual growth for the overall cybersecurity market. Okta and Tenable are expected to grow at roughly 10% and 7%, respectively. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) fell about 4.45% on Friday, while the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW) fell nearly 4.33%. Blockstream CEO Adam Back said the next big wave of Bitcoin (BTC) buying will come from professional money managers such as pension funds and insurers, adding that this phase is "still largely to come." During an interview with Bitcoin Magazine on Saturday, Back, the inventor of Hashcash, said Bitcoin's first wave of adoption came from "individuals mining or buying Bitcoin OTC or on Bitcoin exchanges." He added that "then, the ETFs brought in a second wave." Spot exchange-traded funds opened Bitcoin up to investors who were used to buying assets through a broker or financial adviser. The third wave, he said, will come through large pools of capital run by professionals. Back noted that several large investment banks have "proposed model portfolios where they would suggest 2 to 4% allocation to Bitcoin." Those allocations could flow into mutual funds that individuals pay into for long-term savings, or "be used by pension funds," he said. Back said that is how many people will end up owning Bitcoin without buying it themselves. "For most people, they are not managing their own investments," he said. Instead, their money is invested "by professional money managers in pension funds, insurance companies, life insurance policies." He added that Bitcoin treasury companies are also part of that picture, since some of those funds buy shares of publicly listed firms that hold Bitcoin. Back said regulation still limits how easily traditional institutions can hold Bitcoin. He pointed to bank capital rules, under which holding Bitcoin for clients "uses up a lot of tier one capital. So, it's quite expensive for them." He said that comes down to global Basel banking rules, which are still adapting to the asset. Back also noted that major custodians of stocks and bonds are starting to move into Bitcoin custody, helped by rule changes in the U.S. over the past year. Bitcoin's price was up 0.7% over 24 hours.
